name: Scaling Oversight: From Demonstrations to AI Feedback
claim: Concrete Problems (2016) poses limited human oversight as an open problem and names reward hacking and Goodhart's law as its central failure mode; InstructGPT (2022) answers it with human demonstrations, ranked preference labels, and a learned reward model; Constitutional AI (2022) extends the same lineage by replacing human harmlessness labels with AI feedback judged against a written constitution, and each stage re-encounters the reward-hacking problem named in 2016.
narrative: Concrete Problems in AI Safety (2016) opens by defining accidents as harm from a poorly specified objective and shows how a written reward gets gamed, a pattern it names Goodhart's law. Alongside structural fixes for side effects and unsafe exploration, it proposes semi-supervised reward learning and learning from demonstrations as ways to scale human oversight beyond what a designer can check by hand. InstructGPT (2022) builds directly on the demonstrations proposal: contractors write example completions, then rank model outputs, and those preference labels train a reward model that stands in for further human judgment during reinforcement learning. Constitutional AI (2022) extends the same lineage again, replacing human harmlessness labels with a feedback model that judges outputs against a written constitution. At each stage the corpus's own measurements, reward-model over-optimization, hedging, evasiveness, show the learned proxy diverging from what it was meant to track, exactly as Concrete Problems' account of Goodhart's law predicts.

children.name: Reward Hacking and Goodhart's Law
children.narrative: Concrete Problems (2016) frames its subject as accidents, harm from poor design, deliberately distinct from speculative superintelligence risk and from adjacent fields such as privacy, fairness, and security research. Its central failure mode is reward hacking: an agent that satisfies a written objective's letter while defeating its intent, caused by partial observability, complex systems, abstract rewards, feedback loops, or an agent able to reach its own reward channel. Proposed defenses split into adversarial-ML transplants, adversarial reward functions, adversarial blinding, counterexample resistance, and conventional engineering fixes, model lookahead, reward capping, trip wires. Concrete Problems names the underlying principle Goodhart's law: a proxy optimized directly stops tracking the goal it once correlated with. InstructGPT (2022) and Constitutional AI (2022) each rediscover this pattern empirically, as reward-model over-optimization and as what Constitutional AI calls Goodharting behavior.

Side Effects and Safe Exploration
children.narrative: Concrete Problems (2016) addresses two accident types that do not depend on scaling human oversight. Negative side effects are tackled by penalizing an agent for moving the environment away from a baseline state, by limiting its potential influence rather than its realized actions, or by treating side effects as a relationship to other agents' interests, as in cooperative inverse reinforcement learning. Safe exploration is tackled by confining an agent to regions known to be safe or recoverable, through simulated or bounded exploration or human sign-off, and by replacing expected-value objectives with risk-sensitive criteria. Formal verification and control-theory tools, reachability analysis, H-infinity control, model repair, recur across both problem areas as technical substrate. These safeguards are engineered into the system in advance, in contrast to the ongoing human-feedback mechanisms InstructGPT and Constitutional AI build later.

Learning from Demonstrations
children.narrative: Concrete Problems (2016) proposes learning from demonstrations as a remedy for reward hacking and unsafe exploration: an agent can learn a policy or reward function from expert trajectories via inverse reinforcement learning or apprenticeship learning, instead of optimizing a hand-specified objective. InstructGPT (2022) operationalizes this directly as the first stage of its pipeline: supervised fine-tuning trains GPT-3 on roughly 13,000 human-written demonstrations of desired behavior, producing the SFT model used both as a baseline and as the initialization for later stages. The paper argues this instruction-following objective is what users actually want, against the standard next-token prediction objective and prior instruction-tuning baselines such as FLAN and T0. What began in 2016 as one option among several for avoiding specification failure becomes, in 2022, the concrete first step of a working alignment pipeline.

Preference Labels and the Reward Model
children.narrative: Concrete Problems (2016) names scalable oversight as the problem of evaluating a true objective too costly to check on every example, and proposes semi-supervised reward learning, predicting reward on unlabeled episodes, plus distant supervision and hierarchical decomposition as routes that do not require a learned predictor. InstructGPT (2022) operationalizes this lineage at scale, without using the term: contractors write demonstrations and rank model outputs, and those comparisons train a reward model, a learned proxy for human preference, that PPO then optimizes, with a per-token KL penalty holding the policy near its supervised starting point. Constitutional AI (2022) later reads InstructGPT's reward model back through this same lineage, citing it as a step toward what it calls 'scaled supervision,' where an AI preference model substitutes for immediate human oversight.

AI Feedback and the Written Constitution
children.narrative: Constitutional AI (2022) extends the scalable-oversight lineage further, replacing human harmlessness labels with feedback from the model itself. A written constitution drives two stages: supervised learning, in which the model critiques and revises its own harmful responses to produce SL-CAI, and reinforcement learning from AI feedback, in which a feedback model, engineered with chain-of-thought prompting and calibrated multiple-choice comparisons, judges response pairs against the constitution to generate harmlessness preference labels. Those labels combine with human-labeled helpfulness comparisons into a hybrid preference model, otherwise trained exactly as InstructGPT's reward model. The harmful prompts come from human red-teaming. Constitutional AI positions its method against prior dialogue agents, closest to Sparrow's rule-based harmlessness decomposition, and shares the helpful-honest-harmless framework InstructGPT also uses, adapted from Askell et al.

Measuring What Oversight Produced
children.narrative: InstructGPT (2022) and Constitutional AI (2022) both need to measure whether their trained models are actually better, and each combines automatic overlap metrics, ROUGE, BLEU, F1, with human or model judgment, win rate, Likert ratings, Elo scores. InstructGPT checks its models against public NLP, translation, and summarization benchmarks to catch the alignment tax RLHF imposes on general capability, and against TruthfulQA, RealToxicityPrompts, and bias benchmarks to catch harms capability scores would miss; it also documents remaining failures, hallucination, excessive hedging, reward-model over-optimization. Constitutional AI tracks a documented tradeoff in which harmlessness training tends to make models more evasive, and reports that Constitutional RL shifts the whole helpfulness-harmlessness frontier outward rather than simply trading one for the other, its central empirical claim.

Distributional Shift
children.narrative: Concrete Problems (2016) closes with robustness to distributional shift: an ML system should perform reasonably, and know when it is performing badly, once deployed on a distribution unlike its training one, the assumption every oversight mechanism examined earlier depends on implicitly, since demonstrations, preference labels, and reward models are all captured on one distribution and applied on another. The paper proposes two families of response: relaxing which statistical assumptions must hold across training and test, as in covariate shift correction, partially specified models, or unsupervised risk estimation, or reframing the problem entirely, either causally, as counterfactual reasoning about what would have happened under a different distribution, or as machine learning built to explicit behavioral contracts rather than an implicit assumption that training and deployment match. Neither InstructGPT nor Constitutional AI directly revisits this problem.

children.name: Weakening statistical assumptions to survive distribution shift
Reframing distributional shift as broken contracts and causal structure

intro:
Something has to check what the model produced, and this corpus changes who or what that is at every stage: a human writing an example, then ranking outputs, then a reward model, then an AI judging against a written constitution. Each handoff re-encounters the failure Concrete Problems named in 2016: a proxy drifting from its target.

The chapters climb that ladder: reward hacking and Goodhart's law, side effects and exploration set aside, demonstrations, preference labels and the reward model, AI feedback and the constitution, how results were measured, and distributional shift, untouched by any rung. Open one chapter at a time; the tree's controls set the zoom.
